body:
There is no single age when every baby needs to move from a bassinet to a crib.

The right time depends on your baby and the bassinet you use. In general, it is time to make the switch when your baby reaches the bassinet's weight, height, or developmental limit; starts becoming more mobile; or is simply running out of room.

The most important first step is to check your bassinet's manual. Its limits matter more than a generic age recommendation.

And moving to a crib does not mean your baby has to move out of your bedroom. If you are still room-sharing, a crib can be used in the same room.

1. Your baby has reached the bassinet's limit

This is the clearest reason to stop using a bassinet.

Check the manufacturer's instructions for:

  • maximum weight
  • maximum height, if one is listed
  • developmental milestones that require you to stop using it

Some bassinets should no longer be used once a baby can push up, roll, or reach another specific mobility milestone—even if they are still below the maximum weight.

Once your baby reaches any of the manufacturer's limits, it is time to move to another approved sleep space.

2. Your baby is becoming more mobile

Babies can become stronger surprisingly quickly.

Rolling attempts, pushing up, scooting, pivoting, and stronger kicking are all good reasons to check whether your bassinet is still appropriate for your baby's stage.

You do not necessarily need to wait until a new skill is fully mastered. If your baby is approaching a developmental cutoff listed by the bassinet manufacturer, planning the crib transition early can prevent an abrupt change later.

3. The bassinet is getting cramped

A baby can still fall asleep well in a bassinet that they are beginning to outgrow.

Look at how much usable room your baby has to stretch, move, and reposition. If they constantly brush against the sides or look increasingly crowded, a full-size crib may simply be a better fit for the next stage.

The manufacturer's limits still come first, but physical fit can be another useful clue that the bassinet stage is coming to an end.

4. You know the transition is coming soon anyway

You do not need to wait until the bassinet becomes unusable overnight.

If your baby is close to a weight or developmental limit, setting up the crib ahead of time can make the transition much less stressful.

That way, you can make the change while bedtime is relatively predictable instead of discovering after a new milestone that you suddenly need a different sleep setup that night.

Check the manual before following an age guideline

Parents often search for an exact age to move from bassinet to crib, but bassinets are not all designed for the same length of use.

One model may have a different weight limit or developmental cutoff than another.

That is why your bassinet's instructions should be your main reference. Check the manual for:

  • weight limits
  • height limits
  • rolling or pushing-up restrictions
  • any other developmental cutoff

If you no longer have the manual, look up the exact model before continuing to use the bassinet.

The fact that your baby still sleeps comfortably in it does not override the manufacturer's safety limits.

You can move to a crib and keep room-sharing

Moving from a bassinet to a crib and moving your baby into a separate bedroom are two different decisions.

If you want to continue room-sharing, you can place the crib in your bedroom as long as you have enough space to use it safely.

Before buying or moving a crib, measure the room rather than relying on the product dimensions alone. Think about the space you need to:

  • walk around the crib
  • get in and out of bed
  • handle nighttime feeds
  • reach anything you regularly use overnight

A crib that technically fits but blocks your normal movement can quickly become frustrating.

How to make the bassinet-to-crib transition easier

You do not need to change your baby's entire bedtime routine just because the sleep space changes.

Keeping familiar cues can make the crib feel like a new location within an otherwise familiar routine.

Try to:

  • set up the crib before you urgently need it
  • keep bedtime at roughly the same time
  • continue using the same sleep sack if your baby already uses one
  • keep familiar lighting and sound-machine routines
  • use a firm, properly fitting crib mattress with a fitted sheet
  • keep the crib free of loose blankets, pillows, bumpers, and other soft items

If possible, introduce the crib before your baby has completely outgrown the bassinet. That gives you more flexibility if the first few nights take some adjustment.

What actually matters when choosing the next crib

Cribs often come with long lists of features, but only a few will meaningfully affect everyday use.

Safety and mattress fit

Start with the basics.

Choose a crib that meets current U.S. safety requirements and use a firm mattress that fits the crib properly without large gaps around the edges.

These are more important than decorative features or nursery trends.

Adjustable mattress height

An adjustable mattress platform can make the crib easier to use across different developmental stages.

A higher setting may make it easier to place a younger baby into the crib. As your baby becomes more mobile and begins pulling up, the mattress can be lowered according to the crib manufacturer's instructions.

The right size for your room

If you plan to keep room-sharing, measure carefully before choosing a crib.

A full-size crib offers more long-term use, but the best option is still one that fits your actual space without making nighttime routines difficult.

Sturdy construction

A crib should feel stable and well built.

This becomes increasingly important as your baby grows, moves more, and eventually begins standing and pulling on the rails.

Materials and certifications

Some parents also prioritize lower-emission materials or certifications such as GREENGUARD Gold when choosing nursery furniture.

If that matters to your family, it can be a useful way to narrow your choices after the essential safety and fit requirements are covered.

Convertibility

A convertible crib can make sense if you want one piece of furniture to last into the toddler years.

But convertibility is only valuable if you expect to use it. Check what conversion pieces are included and whether any additional rails or kits need to be purchased separately.

A well-built convertible crib, including options from brands such as Dadada Baby, can be worth considering if long-term use, materials, and design are priorities for your nursery.

The bottom line

You do not need to wait until your baby is obviously too big for the bassinet.

Check the bassinet's manufacturer limits first. If your baby is approaching a weight, height, or developmental cutoff—or is becoming noticeably more mobile or cramped—it may be time to prepare the crib.

And if you still want your baby nearby at night, the transition does not have to end room-sharing. The crib can simply become the next sleep space in the same room.

    FAQ

    Can a baby move from bassinet to crib before 6 months?

    Yes. Babies do not need to stay in a bassinet until 6 months if the bassinet is nearing its limits or no longer fits the baby well. A crib can be the safer option earlier, including in the parents’ room. The key is to follow your bassinet’s product-specific limits and keep safe-sleep basics consistent.

    Can we keep room-sharing after moving to a crib?

    Yes. Moving to a crib does not mean you must move your baby into a separate nursery right away. Many families place a crib in the parents’ room and continue room-sharing there, which can make the transition feel much less abrupt.

    What if my baby still sleeps great in the bassinet?

    That can happen right up until the bassinet is no longer the best fit. Good sleep does not cancel out size limits, milestone limits, or a tighter sleep space. If your baby is getting bigger, stronger, or more mobile, it is worth planning the crib move before there is a same-night safety concern.

    Which crib features are worth paying more for?

    The upgrades most likely to matter are sturdiness, adjustable mattress height, healthy-material considerations, and convertibility that you expect to use. Those features support safety, easier daily use, and better long-term value. If you want one purchase to carry this transition well, a durable convertible crib made with low-emissions materials is usually money better spent than trendy extras.

    Do I need to wait for obvious rolling before I switch?

    No. It is often smarter to move when rolling or pushing up seems close, not only after it is fully established. This is one of those transitions where acting early usually feels calmer than reacting late.
